projects.impact: About 300 ms from data fetch to display, the fastest election results in Brazil.
projects.story:
# Brazilian Elections 2026 at CNN Brasil

I was tech lead for the election results data pipeline at CNN Brasil, working through setup.news as the bridge between editorial and engineering.

### What we built

- Ingestion of official results from the TSE (Superior Electoral Court) API
- Validation rules and a live fallback, so bad or late data never reached air
- Delivery of the same results to TV graphics, web and social

# Results

- **About 300 ms** from fetching the TSE data to showing it on screen
- The fastest election results display in Brazil

projects.title: CNN Brasil Magic Wall
projects.summary: Touch wall for CNN Brasil's 2026 election coverage: four offices, every state and municipality, 2018 and 2022 history, and results that animate in as the presenter navigates.
projects.impact: President, Governor, Senate and Chamber on one 1920×1080 touch stage, down to every municipality, fed live from the official TSE files.
projects.story:
# What it is

A touch wall for CNN Brasil's 2026 election coverage, delivered through setup.news. One 1920×1080 stage, four offices (President, Governor, Senate, Chamber), every state and every municipality, with the results animating in as you navigate.

![The 2026 presidential result by state, with each state coloured by its leading party and the top candidates ranked beside the map](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-1.jpg)

# How a presenter drives it

- A left rail picks the office and the state; inside a state it becomes an A to Z index of municipalities
- Tap the map to drill down: every municipality coloured by its winner, with the municipal count of ballot boxes
- Archive tabs replay 2018 and 2022, first and second round, on the same map
- Capitals mode marks every state capital and opens its vote with one tap

![Tapping a state swaps the map for its municipalities, and an A to Z index opens any city's result, here Campinas](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-2.jpg)

![The 2018 and 2022 tabs replay past presidential races, first or second round, on the same map](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-3.jpg)

![Capitals mode marks every state capital on the map, and tapping a state opens its capital's vote, here Salvador](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-4.jpg)

# Every office

![The governor view sorts the 27 states into races decided in the first round and races going to a runoff](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-5.jpg)

![A state's governor race, with its municipal map and the leading candidates](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-6.jpg)

![A semicircle of the 81 seats shows the Senate's 2027 makeup by party](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-7.jpg)

![A 513-seat hemicycle with seats by party; tapping a party lists its elected deputies by vote](/assets/projects/magicwall/fig-8.jpg)

# Motion

Every change is animated: maps grey out and refill with the new colours, numbers count up from zero, cards slide in, the Senate arc and the Chamber hemicycle build seat by seat. A URL flag turns animation off for rehearsals, and a simulator data source with self-changing fictional numbers tests the animations before election night.

<video controls preload="metadata" poster="/assets/projects/magicwall/banner.jpg" style="width: 100%;">
  <source src="/assets/projects/magicwall/demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

# Data path

The wall reads the official TSE result files, mirrored with the TSE's own paths, plus processed layers on the same results API: national summaries, municipal winners, Chamber seat projections, 2018 and 2022 history and candidate photos. Live updates arrive over MQTT, with polling every 5 seconds as the fallback. The app itself is a static React and GSAP build on Bunny CDN.

# Results

- 2026 first round complete on the wall: 499,248 ballot boxes nationally
- President, Governor, Senate and Chamber, all 27 states, every municipality
- 2018 and 2022 presidential history, both rounds, on the same map

projects.title: Apuração 2026
projects.summary: Real-time election results app for Brazil 2026: follow races live, drill from the map down to every municipality, open any candidate's page, and see the new Congress fill in. Served from a CDN mirror of the official TSE files.
projects.impact: Official results mirrored to object storage behind a CDN, so readers and newsrooms never hit the TSE directly, including municipal results for 2026 and 2022.
projects.story:
# The problem

On election night everyone hits the same official source at the same time. The TSE publishes results as static JSON files, and it rate-limits heavy readers.

# The solution

Apuração reads the TSE once and serves everyone else from a CDN.

- A **mirror service** follows the official result files and copies them into object storage, keeping the TSE's own paths
- A **CDN pull zone** (`api.apuracao.setup.news`) fronts the bucket, so the web app, newsroom graphics and maps read cached files
- **Historical layers** sit next to the live ones: 2022 results by municipality and simplified municipal geometry, ready for maps

![One read from the TSE, served to everyone: a mirror copies the official files to storage and a CDN serves the app, TV graphics and maps](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-5.jpg)

The app lets readers choose the races they follow (president, governor by state, candidates by name or number) and notifies them when results come in.

![Three steps on a phone: pick the races, get the alert, read the result](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-1.jpg)

![The Real time screen follows each race you picked, here President and São Paulo governor, with the share of sections counted](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-2.jpg)

![The full results page adds turnout, blank and null votes, and the most voted candidate by state](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-3.jpg)

![The map view shows the governor races by state: elected in the first round, or going to a runoff](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-4.jpg)

# What's inside

Five tabs, all fed by the same mirrored files and refreshed every 10 seconds on election night.

- **Real time**: the races you follow, with the share of sections counted
- **Resultados**: every race in all 27 states, from President to State Deputy, with turnout, blank and null votes and who the electorate is by sex and age
- **Mapa**: President, Governor and Senate by state, with a drill-down to every municipality and a 2026/2022 toggle
- **Congresso**: the new Senate and Chamber filled seat by seat, by party
- **Candidatos**: a page per candidate with result, map, profile, electoral history, declared assets and campaign accounts from TSE open data

![Every state drills down to its municipalities: Minas Gerais split 452 to 401 between PT and PL in the presidential vote](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-7.jpg)

![Tap a municipality for its own result, and switch to 2022 to compare](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-8.jpg)

![Each candidate has a page with their 2026 result, a map of where they did best, and their profile from TSE records](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-9.jpg)

![On a phone, a candidate page scrolls from profile and result to electoral history, declared assets and campaign accounts](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-10.jpg)

![The Congress view fills the Chamber seat by seat: 513 of 513 deputies elected, by party](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-11.jpg)

![The same depth on mobile: map by state, map by municipality, and the new Congress](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-12.jpg)

<video controls preload="metadata" poster="/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-2.jpg" style="width: 100%;">
  <source src="/assets/projects/apuracao/demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

# Results

- Live 2026 results by municipality served without touching the TSE
- The same feed powers the Urnas map and swing analyses on election night

![The final first-round count for President, from the app's own data: 499,248 of 499,248 sections](/assets/projects/apuracao/fig-6.jpg)

projects.title: OGraf.dev
projects.summary: The community home of OGraf, the EBU's open format for broadcast graphics: one web-native package that plays on any compatible renderer, with no vendor lock-in.
projects.impact: v1 stable since September 2025; 10+ tools and renderers; adopters include Adobe, BBC, NRK, Deutsche Welle and CBC.
projects.story:
# Why it matters

Broadcast graphics have always been tied to the engine that renders them. OGraf, an open specification backed by the European Broadcasting Union, changes the unit of exchange: a graphic is a web package that any compliant renderer can play.

![Where OGraf fits in: the site's comparison of cross-renderer portability against Vizrt, Chyron, Ross, Avid, Flowics and Singular](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-4.jpg)

# What ograf.dev is

I curate ograf.dev with the OGraf community. It is the practical entry point to the spec for designers, developers and broadcasters.

![The ograf.dev home page: a community guide to OGraf, the EBU's open format for broadcast graphics](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-1.jpg)

- **11 production tutorials**: lower thirds, tickers, quotes and more
- A map of the **tools and renderers** that already speak OGraf (SPX Graphics, Loopic, SuperFlyTV, StreamShapers, CasparCG, ograf-server)
- Spec, history and news in English, Portuguese and Spanish

![Four of the 11 production tutorials, each a working OGraf graphic in the site's live preview](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-3.jpg)

# How a graphic flows

A graphic is a **Web Component** with standard lifecycle methods plus a **JSON Schema** describing its data. It is validated against the EBU schema and then plays on any OGraf renderer, with no proprietary runtime.

![The first tutorial pairs the package's manifest.json with the graphic playing live, with Play, Update and Stop](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-2.jpg)

![One OGraf package going to air on CasparCG, SPX, ograf-server and Loopic](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-6.jpg)

# Results

- v1 stable since September 2025
- 10+ tools and renderers
- Adopters include Adobe, BBC, NRK, Deutsche Welle and CBC

![Vendors and broadcasters supporting the spec, from Adobe to the BBC, NRK, Deutsche Welle and CBC](/assets/projects/ograf/fig-5.jpg)

projects.title: Story Object Model
projects.summary: SOM 1.0, an open standard for story context in content production: one publish/subscribe bus where every newsroom tool reads and writes a single, live description of the story.
projects.impact: Published at IBC 2026 (12 Sep) with 14 champion organisations, including AP, BBC, NBCUniversal and Reuters, and 17 technology participants.
projects.story:
# The problem

A story lives in many tools at once: planning, rundown, graphics, playout, the MAM. Each holds a slightly different version of what is true, and they keep each other in sync through point-to-point integrations.

![The storyobjectmodel.dev home page: one bus for story context, every tool on it](/assets/projects/som/fig-1.jpg)

# The model

SOM puts one layer underneath those tools. **Tools talk to the story, not to each other.**

![Tools talk to the story, not to each other: six roles on one bus, and the three nouns Story, Asset and Telling](/assets/projects/som/fig-2.jpg)

- A **publish/subscribe bus** (broker-agnostic) carrying seven JSON message families with permanent schema URLs
- Three core concepts: **Story**, **Asset** and **Telling**
- **Full snapshots**: omission means absent, and late joiners receive the complete state
- A **skills library** that encodes editorial rules once, readable by every tool
- **Compliance gates** tied to story versions: any hold means held
- Media travels by reference only; content never rides the bus

![Every SOM message shares one closed envelope, with message_type as the only discriminator](/assets/projects/som/fig-3.jpg)

SOM does not replace MOS, the NCS or the MAM. It coordinates context above them.

![Editorial rules are written once as skills every tool can read, and a hold stays held until a person decides](/assets/projects/som/fig-4.jpg)

# My role

I am the author of storyobjectmodel.dev, the public home of SOM 1.0: the concepts, the envelope and message references, the skills rulebook and the getting-started path, in English, Portuguese, Spanish and German.

![From the animation: a warning holds playout until the standards desk clears it](/assets/projects/som/fig-6.jpg)

# Results

- SOM 1.0 published at IBC Amsterdam, 12 September 2026
- Developed in the IBC Accelerator Media Innovation Programme 2026 (SMART STORIES)
- 14 champion organisations and 17 technology participants

![SOM 1.0 was built with fourteen champion organisations and seventeen technology participants through the IBC Accelerator](/assets/projects/som/fig-5.jpg)

projects.title: Urnas 2026
projects.summary: "How the ballot boxes draw the country": the 2026 presidential first round mapped polling place by polling place, rebuilt from the raw ballot-box files and checked against the TSE.
projects.impact: 93,500 polling places and 497,075 sections, reconciled line by line with the official result, and shipped as a static site with a ~1 MB first load.
projects.story:
# The challenge

Official results stop at the municipality. The story of an election is often in the neighbourhood: which schools, which streets, which side of the river. That data exists, since every ballot box publishes its own bulletin (BU), but as hundreds of thousands of small binary files.

![One dot per polling place: 93,500 places and 497,075 sections, coloured by the most voted presidential candidate](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-1.jpg)

# The pipeline

![From raw ballot-box files to a static map: backup, ASN.1 decode, reconcile, geocode, static build, CDN](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-2.jpg)

1. **Backup**: batch download of the ballot-box files for every section, with rate steps and a circuit breaker on 429/403 so the TSE is never hammered
2. **Decode**: an ASN.1 decoder turns each BU into rows (votes and sections) stored as Parquet per state, including sections counted by the backup tally system
3. **Reconcile**: every state is checked against the official result, line by line, before anything is drawn (technical nulls folded into nulls, uninstalled sections accounted for)

![The Sobre os dados panel explains the method; the scoreboard matches the official TSE result](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-3.jpg)
4. **Geocode**: polling places joined to the TSE location register; abroad, where the register has no coordinates, cities are geocoded by name and country

![Abroad, the TSE publishes no coordinates, so the 170 polling places outside Brazil were placed by city and country](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-4.jpg)
5. **Publish**: a light static site: columnar points, detail cards in 183 shards fetched on tap, a custom canvas layer and long-lived CDN caching

![On mobile: the map, a polling-place card fetched on tap and the list of nearby places](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-5.jpg)

# Results

![São Paulo metro: the red periphery and the blue centre, polling place by polling place](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-6.jpg)

![Zoomed into São Paulo, each place shows its result, turnout and every section's ballot box](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-7.jpg)

![Highlighting one state: Minas Gerais splits between a red north and a blue south](/assets/projects/urnas/fig-8.jpg)

- **93,500** polling places and **497,075** sections on one map
- Totals that match the official TSE result
- ~1 MB gzipped first load on mobile

projects.title: Flow Radar
projects.summary: Live 2D football radar from broadcast video: players as team-coloured dots, the ball and smoothed movement, streamed over WebSocket from a serverless GPU.
projects.impact: About 17 fps live on one L4 GPU, about US$1.65 per 90-minute match and US$0 idle. SAM 3 was tested and set aside: detection was never the bottleneck.
projects.story:
# What it is

A live 2D radar for football. The input is broadcast video, the camera that pans, zooms and cuts like on TV. The output is a top-down minimap where every player is a dot coloured by team, with the ball and smoothed movement, streamed in real time over WebSocket from a serverless GPU.

No model trained from scratch: the project is a composition of ready models with the right engineering between them.

![Broadcast with team-classified detections, and the same moment on the 2D radar](/assets/projects/flow-radar/fig-1.jpg)

# Detection was never the bottleneck

YOLOv8 already found about 18 of 22 players. I also tested Meta's **SAM 3**, concept-prompted segmentation, in a one-day spike on an A100: similar detection, much higher cost, a more restrictive licence. For a dot on a map, a silhouette adds nothing, so SAM 3 stayed as a possible future occlusion enhancement, not the base.

What really broke the radar was the **projection**: taking a TV pixel to a real field coordinate. A generic homography collapsed with oblique, partial views, and everyone piled up in the centre circle. Switching to a dedicated field-calibration model, **PnLCalib** (points and lines, fine-tuned on World Cup footage), put players on their real positions. On the test clip, **100% of frames calibrated**.

# Going live: three engineering problems

1. **Stutter.** Calibration costs about 400 ms. Running it inside the frame loop froze the worker. Moving it to a throttled background loop (about 1 Hz, the homography changes slowly) took the live loop from stuttering to **about 17 fps**.
2. **Swapped teams.** The SigLIP + clustering team classifier sampled shirts over a 1 to 2 second window and degenerated. Sampling the same 200 crops spread over time gave a clean 50/50 split. Batching SigLIP per frame cut it from 75 ms to about 30 ms.
3. **Robotic movement.** A 3-second acausal buffer fills gaps when the ball disappears and applies a centred moving average, so trajectories look alive without losing quick plays.

![Tracking held as the camera pans towards the goal](/assets/projects/flow-radar/fig-2.jpg)

# Serverless economics

Everything runs on **Modal**: a GPU function for perception and a web endpoint serving the WebSocket, billed per second only while it runs. A 90-minute match on an L4 costs **about US$1.65**, and idle costs **US$0**.

For the World Cup live demo (Brasil x Marrocos), the stream came in through OBS, and the `/view` fan-out was tuned for about 150 simultaneous viewers behind a Bunny Edge script.

<video controls preload="metadata" poster="/assets/projects/flow-radar/banner.jpg" style="width: 100%;">
  <source src="/assets/projects/flow-radar/demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>

# Results

- About **17 fps** live on a single L4
- About **US$1.65** per 90-minute match, US$0 idle
- 100% of frames calibrated on the Mexico 2-0 South Africa test clip
- Sources, perception, state and transport behind clean interfaces: swapping a file for a live stream is swapping an adapter

projects.title: Riot Games – CBLOL Telemetry 2016
projects.summary: Real-time telemetry system integrating biometric data from players into live eSports broadcasts for Riot Games' CBLOL 2016, connecting Zephyr sensors to Vizrt graphics via custom-built C# software.
projects.impact: Delivered the first human telemetry integration in Brazilian eSports broadcasts, enriching live storytelling under high operational pressure and compliance constraints.
projects.story:
# The Challenge

During the **CBLOL 2016** broadcasts, **Riot Games Brasil** aimed to redefine the eSports viewing experience by introducing **human telemetry**, tracking players’ heart rate, breathing and stress levels to reveal the physical and emotional intensity behind professional gaming.

The initiative took place under **significant pressure from Riot’s production leadership**, as audience numbers were at record highs and expectations for innovation were enormous. Furthermore, strict **compliance and operational safety policies** mandated that no system could interfere with gameplay performance or jeopardize the broadcast, even in case of failure.

The technical environment posed additional challenges: over **2,000 spectators** in the arena, high electromagnetic interference, and numerous wireless devices caused instability in Bluetooth communications.

# The Solution

Working as a **freelance systems engineer**, I developed a two-part telemetry pipeline connecting **Zephyr biometric sensors** worn by the ten players to the **Vizrt** graphics system operated by **wTVision**. The goal was to stream real-time physiological data safely into the broadcast layer without impacting the competition.

Two complementary applications were built in **C#**:

1. **Bluetooth Reader (NUC – Under Stage)**  
   Installed beneath the main stage, this application handled **Bluetooth pairing, decoding, and data normalization** for all ten players’ Zephyr sensors. It managed signal stability and transmitted readings over **TCP Stream**.

2. **Telemetry Controller (Control Room)**  
   Running from the control room, it received data via TCP, processed and formatted it in **JSON**, and sent it via **UDP** to **Vizrt**, where graphics were updated live on screen. It also functioned as a monitoring dashboard, allowing real-time tracking of player vitals.

![System Diagram](/assets/projects/riot-telemetry/diagram.jpg)

# My Role

I was responsible for designing and coding both systems end-to-end:

- Built the **Bluetooth decoding layer** for Zephyr sensors.
- Implemented **TCP/UDP communication middleware** to link stage and control room with minimal latency.
- Developed a **real-time compliance logic** ensuring that signal loss would never impact gameplay or broadcast continuity.
- Supported **live operations** throughout the event, troubleshooting Bluetooth instability under high interference.

<video controls style="width: 100%; border-radius: 1rem; margin: 2rem 0;">
  <source src="/assets/projects/riot-telemetry/demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser does not support the video tag.
</video>

# The Approach

The project was executed in **three weeks**, involving close coordination between **Riot Games**, **wTVision**, and the local production crew. The architecture prioritized **redundancy, reliability, and isolation**, ensuring that any sensor or network failure would not affect live performance.

Although magnetic noise caused **some instability during the event**, the system remained operational and successfully displayed live biometric data throughout the competition, a pioneering moment in Brazilian eSports broadcasting.

# Results

- **First-ever human telemetry integration** in a Brazilian eSports broadcast.
- **Operational compliance** achieved, with no interference with gameplay or broadcast continuity.
- **Functional real-time data visualization** via Vizrt graphics.
- **Performance rated as satisfactory** despite expected signal interference.
- Praised by **Riot Games Brasil** and **wTVision** as an innovative step forward for live eSports production.

![Control Room Screen](/assets/projects/riot-telemetry/screen1.png)

projects.story:
# The platform

setup.news is an AI platform built around journalistic production. It brings the tools a newsroom needs to **discover**, **create** and **distribute** news into one cloud ecosystem.

### Architecture

- **Data Platform**: real-time feeds and 55+ public and market databases (IBGE, Banco Central, TSE, World Bank, INMET weather, sports statistics), normalised once and served to every module
- **Multi-LLM layer**: 400+ models (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek and others) behind a single API and a single contract
- **12 modules** on top: Prompt Press (assistant builder), Transcript, Smart Drive, edge.template (broadcast graphics), edge.engine (overlay/keyer), Magic Wall (interactive studio screen) and more
- **Integrations** with Ardome, AP, vMix, Avid, Premiere and Vizrt

### Operations

- Data residency in Brazil, Europe or the US
- SSO, LGPD compliance, role-based access and a complete audit log

# Results

- **42 ms** real-time data flow
- The data layer behind the CNN Brasil 2026 election pipeline, the Apuração app and the Urnas map

projects.title: Quem Fica em Pé
projects.summary: Game show control system for the Brazilian adaptation of 'Who’s Still Standing?', automating real-time graphics, questions, and prize management for live television broadcast.
projects.impact: Delivered a fully integrated real-time game control suite in two weeks, ensuring flawless live operation and boosting the show's premiere audience ratings on Band.
projects.story:
# The Challenge

In 2012, Rede Bandeirantes brought the international format of *'Who’s Still Standing?'* to Brazil, launching the game show **'Quem Fica em Pé'**, hosted by **José Luiz Datena**. The production demanded a complete digital control ecosystem built from scratch in just **two weeks**, responsible for managing every part of the game’s mechanics in real time.

![Studio Demo](/assets/projects/quemficaempe/demo.jpg)

The system needed to integrate seamlessly with **Vizrt broadcast graphics**, synchronize with the presenter’s timing, and guarantee the accurate calculation of prizes, totaling **over R$500,000** in awards across two seasons. According to the show’s Wikipedia page, the premiere significantly **improved Band’s audience ratings** in the São Paulo region.

# The Solution

A fully custom-built, C#-based platform was developed to manage the entire show logic, with three interconnected applications working in real time:

1. **Game Management System** – Proprietary CMS for registering over **3,000 questions**, managing rounds, prizes, and the complete rundown of each episode.
2. **Vizrt Control Connector** – Real-time TCP socket controller for graphics and animations displayed on the studio’s large screen, ensuring frame-perfect sync with Datena’s narration.
3. **Teleprompter System (TP)** – Interface for presenters and contestants displaying dynamic instructions and timed content during live recording.

 ![SystemScreen](/assets/projects/quemficaempe/tela1.png)

# My Role

I designed the system’s architecture, coded every module, and developed **custom connectors for Vizrt integration**. My responsibilities included:

- Building the CMS and control interfaces
- Implementing the scoring and prize logic
- Managing TCP socket communication between systems

projects.title: BlueMarble
projects.summary: GFS weather tile generator that transforms NOAA meteorological data into interactive web map tiles, featuring 20+ meteorological variables, animated wind effects, and real-time visualization capabilities.
projects.impact: Deep dive into geospatial data processing, mastering GDAL workflows, understanding Web Mercator projections, and building complete data-to-visualization pipelines for meteorological applications.
projects.story:
# The Challenge

Understanding how modern weather mapping services like Windy, Ventusky, or Weather Underground work requires deep knowledge of geospatial data processing, meteorological formats, and web mapping technologies. The challenge was to build a complete pipeline that could:

- **Ingest raw NOAA GFS data** in GRIB2 format (a complex binary meteorological standard)
- **Process 20+ meteorological variables** including temperature, wind, precipitation, clouds, pressure, and specialized metrics like CAPE
- **Transform gridded data into web-ready map tiles** compatible with standard mapping libraries
- **Create visually compelling visualizations** with custom colormaps and transparency handling
- **Optimize performance** for processing large datasets (multi-gigabyte files)

![Weather Map Visualization](/assets/projects/blue-marble/demo.png)

# The Solution

BlueMarble is a comprehensive weather tile generation system that automates the entire pipeline from data download to interactive web visualization. The project demonstrates mastery of geospatial data processing while creating a practical tool for weather visualization.

### Technical Architecture

**Data Pipeline:**
1. **NOAA GFS Data Ingestion** – Automated download of forecast data
2. **GRIB2 Decoding** – Using cfgrib and xarray for data extraction
3. **Variable Processing** – Computing derived metrics (wind speed, apparent temperature)
4. **Geospatial Transformation** – Upsampling and Web Mercator reprojection via GDAL
5. **Tile Generation** – Parallel processing into PNG tiles with custom colormaps
6. **Storage & Delivery** – S3/MinIO deployment for web access

**Advanced Features:**
- **Custom Colormaps:** Specialized color schemes for different weather phenomena
- **Smart Transparency:** Alpha channels for low-value data (clouds <25%, precipitation <0.25mm)
- **Wind Animation:** Particle effects using leaflet-velocity for wind visualization
- **Multi-Layer Support:** Simultaneous overlay of multiple meteorological variables
- **Time Controls:** Interactive playback of forecast sequences

# The Approach

The project was developed as a **personal learning initiative** to understand the complete stack of modern weather visualization:

### Phase 1: Data Understanding
- Studied GRIB2 format specifications
- Analyzed NOAA GFS grid structure and coverage
- Researched meteorological variable standards and units

### Phase 2: Core Pipeline
- Implemented GDAL-based processing workflows
- Developed custom colormaps for each variable type
- Built reprojection and upsampling logic
- Created parallel tile generation system

### Phase 3: Web Integration
- Integrated Leaflet for interactive maps
- Implemented leaflet-velocity for wind animations
- Created responsive controls for layer and time management
- Optimized tile delivery and caching

### Phase 4: Deployment
- Dockerized the entire pipeline
- Implemented S3/MinIO storage integration
- Added memory management and resource limits
- Created comprehensive documentation

# Technology Deep Dive

### Geospatial Processing
- **GDAL (Geospatial Data Abstraction Library):** Industry-standard for raster operations
- **Web Mercator Projection:** EPSG:3857 for web mapping compatibility
- **Tile Pyramid:** Standard zoom levels (0-12) for progressive detail

### Meteorological Data
- **GRIB2 Format:** WMO standard for gridded meteorological data
- **Variable Coverage:** Temperature, humidity, wind (U/V components), precipitation, clouds, pressure, CAPE, and more
- **Temporal Resolution:** 1-hour forecast intervals

### Visualization
- **Matplotlib Colormaps:** Custom and standard schemes (viridis, plasma, jet)
- **Alpha Compositing:** Transparency for data emphasis and layering
- **Canvas Rendering:** HTML5 for smooth particle animations

# Results & Learning Outcomes

**Technical Mastery:**
- Comprehensive understanding of GDAL and geospatial transformations
- Proficiency with xarray and n-dimensional data manipulation
- Knowledge of Web Mercator projection and tile pyramid systems
- Experience with GRIB2 format and meteorological data standards

**System Design:**
- Built scalable data processing pipelines
- Implemented efficient parallel processing
- Designed modular architecture for easy extension
- Created deployment-ready containerized solution

**Web Development:**
- Integrated complex data visualization with Leaflet
- Implemented real-time animation systems
- Optimized asset delivery and caching strategies

**Practical Application:**
- Generated thousands of map tiles from multi-gigabyte datasets
- Created smooth 60fps wind animations
- Achieved memory-efficient processing within Docker constraints
- Built reusable pipeline applicable to other geospatial data sources

# Future Enhancements

Potential extensions include:
- **Additional Data Sources:** ERA5 reanalysis, satellite imagery, radar data
- **Mobile App:** Native iOS/Android weather visualization
- **API Layer:** RESTful service for programmatic access
- **Machine Learning:** Forecast correction and nowcasting models

This project demonstrates the intersection of data engineering, geospatial processing, and web visualization: skills directly applicable to modern mapping platforms, environmental monitoring systems, and data-driven applications.

projects.title: Vizrt Birds
projects.summary: Interactive Angry Birds-style game built entirely in Vizrt's VBA scripting language, applying projectile motion physics and collision detection for touchscreen broadcast graphics. Community-shared tool demonstrating advanced scripting capabilities in VizArtist.
projects.impact: Successfully translated complex physics formulas from Python OOP training into Vizrt's native scripting environment, creating an accessible learning tool for the broadcast graphics community without requiring any plugins.
projects.story:
# The Challenge

In 2015, after completing a Python OOP training course focused on game development and physics simulation, I faced an interesting challenge: **could the projectile motion formulas and collision detection logic I learned in Python be implemented inside Vizrt's broadcast graphics environment?**

The technical hurdles were significant:

- **Language Translation**: Converting Python code to VBA (Vizrt's scripting language)
- **Physics Implementation**: Implementing trajectory calculations without external libraries
- **Interactive Controls**: Creating touchscreen-based gameplay mechanics
- **Performance**: Ensuring smooth real-time animation within Vizrt's rendering pipeline
- **No Plugins**: Building everything using only native VizArtist capabilities for maximum accessibility

![Vizrt Birds Screenshot](/assets/projects/vizbirds/banner.jpg)

# The Solution

**Vizrt Birds** is a fully functional Angry Birds-style game phase built entirely within VizArtist 3.6.3, demonstrating how broadcast graphics software can handle game physics and interactive logic typically reserved for game engines.

### Core Features

**Physics Simulation:**
- **Projectile Motion**: Implemented oblique launch calculations with constant gravity
  - Horizontal position: `X = X₀ + v·cos(θ)·Δt`
  - Vertical position: `Y = Y₀ + v·sin(θ)·Δt - (G·Δt²)/2`
- **Collision Detection**: Cartesian coordinate-based proximity detection
- **Trajectory Rendering**: Real-time path visualization

**Interactive Gameplay:**
- Touchscreen controls for aiming and launching
- Obstacle destruction mechanics
- Game state management

**Technical Architecture:**
- Pure VBA implementation (no plugins)
- Event-driven scripting for user interactions
- Frame-based animation system
- Modular code structure for extensibility

# The Approach

### Phase 1: Python Training Foundation

I completed the Python Birds training course (now available on [GitHub](https://github.com/ficosta/pythonbirds)), which taught:
- Object-oriented programming principles
- Projectile motion physics and mathematics
- Collision detection algorithms
- Game state management

### Phase 2: Physics Translation

The core challenge was translating Python's mathematical operations into VBA:

```python
# Python (from training)
X = X0 + velocity * cos(angle_radians) * delta_time
Y = Y0 + velocity * sin(angle_radians) * delta_time - (GRAVITY * delta_time²) / 2
```

This required:
- Converting trigonometric functions to VBA syntax
- Implementing radian-degree conversions
- Creating custom physics update loops
- Optimizing calculations for real-time performance

### Phase 3: Vizrt Implementation

Built the complete game logic within VizArtist:
- Created actor classes (birds, obstacles, targets)
- Implemented state machines (ACTIVE, LAUNCHED, DESTROYED)
- Developed touchscreen interaction handlers
- Added visual feedback and animation systems

### Phase 4: Community Release

Published on the Vizrt Forum (April 9, 2015) with:
- Complete VIA scene file for download
- No external dependencies or plugins
- Documentation for learning and customization
